results.title: Management Strategies for Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is one of the most debilitating neuropathic facial pain disorders. Although carbamazepine remains the first-line pharmacologic therapy, many patients become refractory or intolerant to long-term medication, necessitating surgical intervention. Multiple operative techniques are available; however, comparative durability and complication profiles remain heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, recurrence rates, and safety of pharmacologic and surgical management strategies for TN.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
<jats:p>A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases including PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating medical and surgical treatments of TN. Randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and systematic reviews reporting measurable pain outcomes were included. Primary outcomes were immediate pain relief and long-term pain freedom (≥3 y). Secondary outcomes included recurrence rates, sensory complications, and quality-of-life measures.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Twenty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Carbamazepine demonstrated effective initial pain control but limited long-term durability due to adverse effects and recurrence. Microvascular decompression (MVD) provided the highest immediate relief (94%) and durable long-term pain freedom (72%). Percutaneous procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizotomy) showed high initial relief (85%–91%) but increased recurrence and sensory morbidity. Stereotactic radiosurgery demonstrated moderate long-term control with low perioperative morbidity but delayed onset of action. Outcomes in multiple sclerosis-associated TN were inferior compared with classic TN.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Microvascular decompression remains the gold standard surgical intervention for medically refractory classic TN in appropriate candidates. Percutaneous and radiosurgical techniques offer effective alternatives for elderly or medically compromised patients. Standardized outcome reporting and high-quality comparative trials are required to refine treatment algorithms.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Validation study of the predictive Comprehensive Longitudinal Investigation of MS at the Brigham and Women's Hospital (CLIMB) model for 10-year multiple sclerosis disease progression using the Ottawa Hospital cohort
results.summary:
Mult Scler Relat Disord. 2026 Nov 15;117:108067. doi: 10.1016/j.msard.2026.108067. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

PURPOSE OF THE RESEARCH: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex disease where patient outcomes range from relatively benign to an aggressive or progressive course. A predictive model developed from the Comprehensive Longitudinal Investigation of MS at the Brigham and Women's Hospital (CLIMB) cohort identified clinical variables that reliably predicted 10-year outcomes but has not been validated in an external cohort. This retrospective validation study assessed 10-year outcomes of retaining benign MS, developing aggressive MS, and developing secondary progressive MS (SPMS) in a new Canadian cohort.

PRINCIPAL RESULTS: A total of 166 patients were included with similar characteristics as CLIMB: 71% were female, the mean (±standard deviation) age was 34.3 ± 9.6years, and the mean initial EDSS was 1.9 ± 1.2. At 10 years, 127 (76.5%) patients retained a benign MS status, 36 (21.6%) patients developed SPMS, and 15 (9.0%) patients developed aggressive MS. The sensitivity of the model was 48.0%, 75.0%, and 86.7%, for benign MS, SPMS, and aggressive MS with area under curve values of 0.71, 0.71 and 0.68, respectively.

MAJOR CONCLUSIONS: The CLIMB model predicted SPMS and aggressive MS with high sensitivity but overcalled a proportion who remained benign, while patients who were identified as remaining benign were unlikely to develop SPMS or aggressive MS.

results.title: AI-assisted longitudinal MRI assessment in multiple sclerosis: diagnostic performance and reduction in reporting time
results.summary: Purpose Detection of new and enlarging lesions on longitudinal MRI is essential for monitoring disease activity in multiple sclerosis (MS) but is time-consuming and subject to inter-reader variability. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance and workflow impact of a CE-marked artificial intelligence (AI) platform compared with neuroradiologists of different experience. Methods In this retrospective study, 59 patients with relapsing–remitting MS underwent baseline and follow-up brain MRI including 3D FLAIR sequences. Two neuroradiologists independently assessed examinations for new or enlarging lesions, blinded to AI output. The reference standard was an AI-blinded consensus of the two readers, with discordant cases adjudicated by an independent third neuroradiologist. Patient-level diagnostic performance was evaluated for each reader alone, the AI alone, and each reader assisted by AI. Agreement was assessed with Cohen’s kappa and reading times with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results Among unassisted assessments, the experienced reader achieved the highest accuracy (88.1%), followed by the less experienced reader (83.1%) and the AI alone (79.7%). AI assistance was associated with higher accuracy for both readers (94.9%, κ = 0.90, and 89.8%, κ = 0.80, respectively). AI assistance significantly reduced reading time for both readers (median within-patient reduction 0.9 and 1.0 min; p < 0.001), independently of baseline T2 lesion volume. Conclusion Against an AI-blinded consensus reference standard, AI assistance was associated with higher diagnostic performance of both readers, irrespective of experience, and significantly reduced reading time, supporting its role as a decision-support tool in the longitudinal MRI assessment of MS.

results.title: 20-year trends in multiple sclerosis prevalence, incidence and age at death in Lombardy, Northern Italy: a region-wide cohort study using administrative linked data
results.summary:
Lancet Reg Health Eur. 2026 Nov 5;72:101921. doi: 10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101921. eCollection 2027 Jan.

ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a leading cause of non-traumatic neurological disability in young adults. We assessed 20-year trends in MS prevalence, incidence and mean age at death in Lombardy, Italy, using population-wide linked administrative data.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study including all regional residents aged 18 years or older between 2005 and 2024. MS cases were identified through an administrative algorithm. Annual crude and age-standardised incidence and prevalence rates were calculated overall and by sex and age group, using the 2025 WHO World Standard Population, including female-to-male ratios. Mean age at death was computed and stratified by sex. Temporal trends were analysed using joinpoint regression.

FINDINGS: Among 10 million residents, MS incidence and prevalence increased from 8.2 (95%CI, 7.6-8.8) to 10.9 (10.2-11.6) and from 71.6 (70.0-73.2) to 152.4 (150.1-154.8) per 100,000 population, respectively, over the period 2005-2024. MS incidence was consistently higher among females and rose most markedly among adults 18-29-year +43.9%, from 12.4 (10.5-14.5; n = 153) to 17.8 (15.5-20.4; n = 217) per 100,000 and 30-39-year +42.9%, from 17.7 (15.7-19.9; n = 283) to 25.3 (22.5-28.4; n = 288). Overall age-standardised incidence declined non-significantly until 2015 (Annual Percentage Change (APC) -0.69%, 95% CI -7.61 to 0.90) followed by a significant increase thereafter (APC +2.84%, 95% CI 0.94-11.58). Incidence increased steadily in males (APC +1.54%, 95% CI 0.47-2.61), and, among females, rose significantly from 2013 onward (APC +2.30%, 95% CI 0.89-8.83). Over the study period, the female-to-male incidence rate ratio decreased from 2.4 (95% CI, 2.0-2.8) to 1.7 (1.5-1.9), whereas the corresponding prevalence ratio changed from 2.1 (95% CI, 2.0-2.2) to 1.9 (1.9-2.1). Mean age at death increased by about 6-10 years linearly since 2005, reaching 69.6 years (median 71.0, IQR 61.0-78.0, SD 11.7) among males and 73.8 years (75.0, 66.5-81.0, 10.7) among females in 2024.

INTERPRETATION: MS incidence and prevalence increased over two decades, particularly among younger adults alongside older age at death. These findings may reflect changing disease risk, improved diagnostic sensitivity, and advances in treatment. Continuous surveillance using linked administrative data is essential for healthcare planning and resource allocation.

FUNDING: None.

results.title: DenseGated-MSNet: A Multi-Sequence Gated Fusion Network for Multiple Sclerosis Classification from Brain MRI
results.summary: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a central role in its diagnosis and monitoring. Because different MRI sequences provide complementary information about MS-related pathology, jointly exploiting multiple sequences may improve automated classification. However, many existing automated MS classification studies rely on limited sequence information, are not consistently evaluated under subject-independent protocols, and are constrained by the scarcity of publicly available multi-sequence datasets organized at the subject level. Methods: To address these gaps, we collected and publicly released a new multi-sequence brain MRI dataset and proposed DenseGated-MSNet, a novel end-to-end multi-input deep learning model for MS versus non-MS classification. DenseGated-MSNet processes each co-acquired MRI sequence in parallel through an independent sequence-specific DenseNet-121 branch and integrates the resulting representations through a proposed input-dependent gated feature-level fusion mechanism. Under a strict subject-independent evaluation protocol, the model configuration was determined on a subject-independent development set, and the performance of the final model was internally evaluated using five-fold subject-independent cross-validation on the same cohort at the image and subject levels. Results: In internal five-fold subject-independent cross-validation, DenseGated-MSNet achieved a pooled subject-level accuracy of 90.57% (95% CI: 86.44–93.53%) and an AUC of 0.947 (95% CI: 0.918–0.976). The learned gate values also provided sequence-level modulation information, indicating how strongly each MRI sequence was weighted during multi-sequence integration. Conclusions: Overall, these findings suggest that DenseGated-MSNet can effectively integrate complementary information from multiple MRI sequences for discriminating established MS from selected non-MS controls, while providing sequence-level modulation information. Together with the released dataset, the proposed framework provides a reproducible basis for future subject-independent MS classification studies.</jats:p>

results.title: Optogenetics in neurobiology and neurodegenerative disorders: from neural circuit mechanisms to precision neuromodulation
results.summary: <jats:p>Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis and stroke, are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment and neural circuit degeneration, leading to severe cognitive and motor deficits. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding their molecular pathology, the circuit level mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain incompletely understood. Optogenetics, which combines microbial opsins, genetic engineering and optical stimulation, enables reversible, cell-specific control of neuronal activity with millisecond precision and has transformed neuroscience from observational analysis to causal investigation of neural circuits. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular basis of optogenetics, microbial opsins, gene delivery strategies and optical stimulation technologies, together with their applications in basic neurobiology and neurodegenerative disease research. We discuss how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, memory, neurodevelopment, sleep regulation, protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death. Although these studies have generated important mechanistic insights and demonstrated functional improvements in experimental models, translation into human therapies remains investigational due to challenges associated with gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and optical accessibility. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including closed-loop neuromodulation, wireless photostimulation, artificial intelligence-assisted neural decoding, nanotechnology enabled light delivery and brain computer interfaces, are critically evaluated with emphasis on their current evidence status, translational challenges and limitations for clinical implementation. Collectively, optogenetics provides an unprecedented platform for deciphering disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based neuromodulation strategies, while continued technological and biological validation will determine its future role in precision therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.</jats:p>

results.title: Artificial intelligence-driven multiple sclerosis diagnosis using genomic and medical imaging data: a review
results.summary: <jats:p>Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated central nervous system condition with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, progressive neurodegeneration, and considerable variability in disease trajectory. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) methods, have improved MS diagnosis and risk prediction. However, comprehensive review studies emphasizing the potential of existing AI-powered MS diagnosis remain limited. Thus, this study investigates the utilization of multimodal data by AI models to enhance diagnostic accuracy, evaluate disease progression, and optimize personalized care strategies. By adhering to PRISMA guidelines, this review included 26 studies encompassing MRI-based analysis, retinal OCT imaging, blood transcriptomics, SNP genotyping, and multimodal clinical datasets. An additional classification of these studies by modality was performed, and they were assessed with respect to dataset size, performance metrics, biomarkers, methodological robustness, and model interpretability. The findings indicate a consistent trend toward outstanding diagnostic performance, with some AI models achieving accuracies exceeding 95% using medical imaging and genomic data. However, limited external validation and interpretability procedures create a gap in clinical applicability and trustworthiness. This review highlights AI's growing potential to revolutionize MS diagnosis.</jats:p>

results.title: Latent Representation Learning from 3D Brain MRI for Latent Analysis and Prediction in Multiple Sclerosis
results.summary: Background: Neurological diseases can lead to significant cognitive impairment. Linking magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived measures of brain structure with clinical assessments of cognitive function remains challenging, as conventional statistical methods and traditional machine learning approaches may struggle to capture complex relationships between brain structure and cognitive outcomes, hindering the development of reliable imaging biomarkers. Although deep learning methods offer greater predictive capabilities, their black-box nature limits interpretability, posing a major obstacle to clinical translation. New method: Latent representation learning via generative models can provide informative representations and support deeper analysis and cognitive biomarker prediction. While standard generative adversarial networks and diffusion models primarily focus on generating images from random noise, variational autoencoders offer compact, probabilistic latent representations that are well suited for downstream tasks. In this study, we propose InfoVAE-Med3D, an adaptation of the InfoVAE framework for three-dimensional brain ​MRI to learn informative latent representations. By explicitly relaxing the mutual information regularization penalty between inputs and latent representations, our method aims to capture richer information from input MRI data, facilitating the analysis of brain-related characteristics and downstream prediction. Results: We evaluate InfoVAE-Med3D on two datasets: a healthy control dataset ($$n=6{,}503$$) containing chronological age and sex information, and a Multiple Sclerosis (MS) dataset ($$n=916$$) collected from the Multiple Sclerosis Center of the First Medical Faculty, Charles University, Prague, containing chronological age, sex, and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) scores. The learned latent representations capture information related to sex and brain volumetric features, including grey and white matter volumes, as reflected in sex-related clustering and smooth transitions in brain volume measures in two-dimensional visualizations. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that InfoVAE-Med3D learns more informative latent representations, especially when the mutual information regularization penalty is completely removed. In this setting, the model generally outperforms other variational autoencoder variants in both MRI reconstruction and prediction of brain age and SDMT scores using support vector regression, while remaining competitive with deep learning-based predictive models, particularly on the MS dataset. Conclusion: InfoVAE-Med3D provides informative latent representations from brain MRI data of both healthy controls and patients with MS. By improving predictive performance and providing interpretable insights into the learned latent representations, the proposed framework offers a promising approach for advancing biomarker discovery and the analysis of cognitive impairment in neurological diseases, particularly ​MS.

results.title: Large language model–enhanced decision tree framework for identifying multiple sclerosis diagnoses from clinical documentation
results.summary:
Mult Scler Relat Disord. 2026 Oct 26;117:108024. doi: 10.1016/j.msard.2026.108024. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND: Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet diagnostic delays are common. Large language models (LLMs) such as generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) may streamline diagnostic workflows by extracting MS diagnostic signals from clinical notes.

OBJECTIVE: To derive MS diagnosis status from the first neurology note using a computable algorithm based on the 2017 McDonald criteria and applying GPT-4 for node-level reasoning within a structured decision framework.

METHODS: We analyzed the first neurology notes from 125 randomly selected patients (people with MS, related disorders, and controls) enrolled in a clinic-based cohort between 2017 and 2023. We included the clinical history and diagnostic testing sections but redacted the assessment and plan. We converted the 2017 McDonald criteria into a decision tree and provided expert-curated clinical knowledge to guide GPT-4 reasoning at each decision node. GPT-4 generated binary decisions at each node to traverse the tree and assign MS diagnoses at terminal nodes. We evaluated performance against neurologist-assessed diagnoses and characterized hallucination types (non-factual, incongruent, irrelevant, over-reliant, and logical reasoning errors).

RESULTS: In this study cohort (mean age 40±12 years; 81% women) representative of the clinic population, GPT-4 performed well in predicting MS diagnosis (84% accuracy, 79% precision, 74% recall, 91% specificity) using first neurology notes. Hallucinations occurred in 32 cases (26%), most commonly incoherence (75%) and overreliance (47%).

CONCLUSION: A structured, LLM-guided decision framework can identify MS diagnoses from early clinical documentation. Large-scale studies are needed to mitigate hallucinations, validate this approach, and test implementation in clinical settings.

results.title: Artificial Intelligence for Brain MRI Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Gap Map Across Neurological Diseases
results.summary:
Curr Med Imaging. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.2174/0115734056523075261026051524. Online ahead of print.

ABSTRACT

INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, is increasingly applied to brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for disease detection, classification, segmentation, and clinically relevant prediction. This review aimed to map the evidence on AI-assisted brain MRI diagnosis, identify methodological and clinical translation gaps, and propose priorities for future research.

METHODS: This scoping review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed English-language publications from January 2018 to April 2026. Data were charted according to disease domain, study design, AI method, dataset, validation strategy, performance metrics, explainability, and key limitations.

RESULTS: The search identified 1,020 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 61 publications were included, comprising 24 original studies used for the primary evidence map and 37 reviews or commentaries used for contextual synthesis. Evidence was strongest for brain tumor imaging and Alzheimer's disease, whereas stroke, multiple sclerosis, pediatric neuroimaging, and rare neurological conditions were underrepresented. Most studies relied on public benchmark datasets and retrospective validation, whereas external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, subgroup analysis, explainability, and workflow integration were inconsistently reported.

DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that AI-assisted brain MRI research remains unevenly developed and is constrained by dataset dependence, limited external validation, limited prospective clinical evaluation, and inconsistent reporting of explainability, subgroup performance, and workflow integration.

CONCLUSION: AI shows promising research-stage potential for brain MRI-based diagnosis, particularly in brain tumor analysis and Alzheimer's disease classification. Future research should prioritize multicenter validation, diverse and disease-specific datasets, explainable and equitable AI design, transparent reporting, and prospective evaluation within real clinical workflows.
